title: Why mandatory payrolling of benefits is proving difficult
label: 29 October 2026 · Mandatory payrolling of benefits in kind
summary: Experts from the professional accountancy and tax bodies explained why requiring employers to report most non-cash employee benefits through payroll (instead of the annual P11D form) is technically and practically hard. Businesses are used to the old annual process, software and data flows aren’t ready, some benefits can’t easily be valued in real time, and HMRC’s phased timetable and data demands risk creating a costly dual system. The witnesses warned that guidance, legislative changes, and realistic timetables are needed to avoid large compliance costs and confusion for employers and employees.

glossary.definition: The annual form employers use to report taxable non-cash employee benefits (for example, private medical insurance or company cars).
Reporting employee benefits through payroll in real time so tax is collected via PAYE rather than on an annual P11D.
A letter HMRC sends to an employee telling them how their tax code has been adjusted, often after new benefits are reported.
Real-Time Information: HMRC's system for regular payroll reporting to collect PAYE data each pay run.
An end-of-year document employers must give employees showing total pay and tax for the year.
Records of money a director owes to—or is owed by—their company; balances can create taxable benefits.
The first set of benefits HMRC plans to require to be payrolled (those it judges easier to report in real time).
Later categories of benefits that HMRC plans to bring in later, often because they are harder to value or report in real time.

chapters.title: Why take-up of payrolling has been low
chapters.takeaway: Businesses have stuck with the annual P11D because it is familiar, often simpler for them, and payrolling looks like a costly transformation.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We are looking at mandatory payrolling of benefits in kind—moving the P11D into payroll—and why take-up since 2016 has been so low.

turns.speaker: Katie Close
turns.text: Many businesses already have P11D processes that work. Making payroll the default is a transformation project: it needs investment, planning and time.

turns.speaker: Sarah Hewson
turns.text: Employers are comfortable with the annual process. The main winners from payrolling are HMRC and employees; employers often see limited benefit.

turns.speaker: Adelle Greenwood
turns.text: Switching needs complete process change and data earlier in the year; that can mean contract changes with benefit providers and extra cost.

turns.speaker: Chris Campbell
turns.text: Some benefits—non-cash ones—have always been suited to the P11D form. Payrolling needs more timely data and coordination across HR, payroll and finance.

chapters.title: Software, data and practical barriers
chapters.takeaway: Payroll software, third-party data, the time demands on staff, and unclear guidance are major obstacles.

turns.speaker: Lord Leigh of Hurley
turns.text: Has HMRC understood why businesses don't want this? Only 16,000 of 280,000 employers have adopted payrolling so far.

turns.speaker: Chris Campbell
turns.text: HMRC has underestimated administration costs, especially early on. If payroll runs weekly, employers may need data many more times a year.

turns.speaker: Katie Close
turns.text: Businesses need certainty far in advance to design and test processes. If things go wrong, employees suffer—so employers are cautious.

turns.speaker: Sarah Hewson
turns.text: HMRC has recognised complexities, which is why it phased the rollout, but there remains a gap in its understanding of employers' challenges.

turns.speaker: Adelle Greenwood
turns.text: Data often arrives after the event; making it available before payroll runs is a big operational change for many firms.

chapters.title: A dual system looks likely and will be complex
chapters.takeaway: Because some benefits can't be valuated in real time, employers will often have to run both payrolled and annual P11D reporting.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: HMRC has accepted some benefits can't be payrolled. Will employers then have to keep both systems, increasing work?

turns.speaker: Sarah Hewson
turns.text: Yes. HMRC accepts a dual process is likely. Phasing is a pragmatic way to proceed, but it does mean extra complexity and cost for employers.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: Can we ever move to a single system?

turns.speaker: Adelle Greenwood
turns.text: Only if how certain benefits are valued changes. The rules for loans and accommodation are written for annual reporting and need legislative change.

turns.speaker: Chris Campbell
turns.text: Phase 1 covers many benefits, but phase 2 and exclusions—like globally mobile employees—mean many employers will still need the P11D route.

turns.speaker: Adelle Greenwood
turns.text: Because directors' loan accounts and other fluctuating items are common, a lot of employers will be affected by exclusions.

chapters.title: Timescales, costs and HMRC's data appetite
chapters.takeaway: The April 2027 timetable, lack of software specs, underestimated employer costs and HMRC's broad data demands threaten the rollout.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: With the dual systems and little software readiness, can HMRC meet its timescales? Eighteen months feels tight.

turns.speaker: Chris Campbell
turns.text: Guidance is paramount. The phased approach should have allowed time, but HMRC hasn't published enough guidance or specifications early enough.

turns.speaker: Sarah Hewson
turns.text: We are five months from April 2027 and still lack software specs. Payroll providers and SMEs will struggle; some large employers may cope.

turns.speaker: Adelle Greenwood
turns.text: Many employers wrongly assume software or bureaux will handle everything. They underestimate internal process changes and data flows.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: Why does HMRC want so much data—more than is clearly needed?

turns.speaker: Sarah Hewson
turns.text: HMRC has asked for many fields—some are arguably unnecessary. It sometimes appears to want data 'in case' it's useful later rather than only what's needed now.

turns.speaker: Adelle Greenwood
turns.text: When RTI fields were first proposed there were 126; they've been cut to 32. But even then, incomplete fields could cause payroll submissions to be rejected.

turns.speaker: Chris Campbell
turns.text: If a required field is missing and an RTI submission is rejected, that can disrupt payroll for all employees, not just those with benefits.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bi
turns.text: Are HMRC's cost estimates for employers realistic?

turns.speaker: Chris Campbell
turns.text: No. Employer costs are likely understated. Getting frequent data from benefit providers will cost money and might prompt providers to charge more.

turns.speaker: Sarah Hewson
turns.text: Payroll changes mean additional steps and likely extra charges for corrected P60s or multiple per-employee submissions when adjustments are needed.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: Does HMRC at least look at cost-benefit for itself?

turns.speaker: Sarah Hewson
turns.text: Yes, HMRC publishes impact assessments, but how accurate they are is unclear. HMRC is focused on long-term data and efficiency gains for itself.

chapters.title: Correction duties and clarity for employers
chapters.takeaway: New correction duties and the obligation to notify HMRC are unclear; guidance must state when to act and how to fix payroll and P11D errors.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: Will the new correction requirement improve compliance?

turns.speaker: Chris Campbell
turns.text: It could, but the law and guidance don't say clearly when a taxpayer is 'aware' of an error and must notify HMRC, or how long they can take to investigate.

turns.speaker: Sarah Hewson
turns.text: Employers need targeted guidance showing step-by-step correction routes for payroll errors and P11D items. Right now the guidance is confusing.

turns.speaker: Adelle Greenwood
turns.text: Many employers use agents; those represented might be prompted to correct issues, but unrepresented employers might not even know about the duty.

turns.speaker: Sarah Hewson
turns.text: A practical surprise example: HMRC treats many immigration-related costs as taxable benefits. Employers often don't realise that until told.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: So employers may be surprised and confused, and the system risks costly corrections and reconciliations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. The witnesses have shown this is a complicated change: software, data, legislation and clearer guidance are needed to avoid burdening employers and employees.
